Spaced Repetition for Kanji: How SRS Actually Works

Kanjidon Team · Jan 29, 2026

A spaced-repetition system is a scheduler, not a memory guarantee. It delays a prompt after successful recall and brings failed material back sooner. Used well, that can reduce unnecessary repetition. Used badly, it can create a large queue of shallow cards that you recognize only inside the app. The goal is not to obey an algorithm; it is to retrieve useful Japanese and still understand it in the wild.

Two Ideas Work Together

Spacing

Studying an item on separate occasions can support longer retention better than compressing the same repetitions into one sitting. The useful gap changes with the desired retention period and with how stable the memory already is, so research does not justify one fixed sequence for every learner or kanji.

Retrieval

A review is most informative when you try to produce the answer before seeing it. Research on retrieval practice shows that repeated successful testing can improve delayed recall more than repeated restudy alone. Recognition after revealing the back of a card is not the same as retrieving the answer.

What an SRS Can—and Cannot—Estimate

A scheduler uses your review history to choose a future date. That date is a practical estimate, not the exact moment you would otherwise forget. Memory is affected by sleep, context, interference, card design and exposure outside the app. Different algorithms also make different assumptions, so “due” should mean “useful to test now,” not “scientifically optimal to the minute.”

Design Kanji Prompts Around One Decision

  • Ask for one answer at a time: a meaning, a reading in a specific word, or production of the written form.
  • Put readings inside vocabulary. 食べる and 食事 provide clearer targets than a card asking for every reading of 食.
  • Use a sentence or image only when it helps identify the intended word without giving the answer away.
  • Separate close look-alikes into contrast prompts, such as 待 and 持.
  • Suspend or rewrite cards that remain ambiguous; repeated failure can be a prompt problem, not a learner problem.

A Sustainable Review Loop

  • Clear a small set of due reviews before adding new material.
  • Answer from memory, reveal the target, and correct the specific error.
  • If you fail, inspect why: shape, meaning, sound, vocabulary or an ambiguous prompt.
  • Meet the item in reading or listening so the card is not its only context.
  • Reduce new cards when daily reviews stop fitting the time you actually have.

Do Not Turn the Buttons into Self-Grading Theatre

Use the failure option when you did not retrieve the target. Choosing a positive grade because the answer “looked familiar” teaches the scheduler that the memory is stronger than it is. At the same time, do not punish minor differences that the prompt never specified. Clear prompts and honest grading matter more than chasing a perfect retention percentage.

How Kanjidon Fits

Kanjidon schedules spaced reviews and can test different faces of kanji and vocabulary through multiple quiz formats. That variety can reveal whether you recognize, recall, hear or write an item. It still works best as part of a broader routine with grammar, listening and real reading; no review algorithm can promise an N5 result in a fixed number of weeks.

Sources and Further Reading

  • Karpicke and Roediger (2008): The Critical Importance of Retrieval for Learning
  • Cepeda et al. (2008): Spacing Effects in Learning
